frontal_pole.name: Frontal pole
frontal_pole.tagline: The very front tip of the brain, involved in planning and juggling goals.
frontal_pole.overview: The frontal pole is the foremost tip of each frontal lobe, sitting just behind the forehead. It belongs to the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain most involved in complex thinking. It is thought to help us keep a main goal in mind while dealing with something else, and to reflect on our own thoughts.
functions: Keeping one goal on hold while working on another
Thinking about one's own thinking and decisions
connections: Other parts of the prefrontal cortex
Temporal lobe areas involved in memory
clinical: Damage here, for example after a head injury, may cause subtle problems with planning and organising rather than obvious weakness or numbness.
Because it lies just behind the forehead, it can be affected when the front of the head is injured.
frontal_pole.lateralization: Both sides work together; there is no well-established split of roles between left and right.
frontal_pole.fact: The prefrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to finish maturing, continuing to develop into early adulthood.
frontal_pole.blood_supply: Mainly the anterior cerebral artery (frontopolar branch), with some supply from the middle cerebral artery on the outer side.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

sfg.name: Superior frontal gyrus
sfg.tagline: The top ridge of the frontal lobe, involved in thinking and controlling movement.
sfg.overview: The superior frontal gyrus is the uppermost of the three long ridges that run front to back along the frontal lobe. It extends over the top of the brain onto its inner (medial) surface. Its back part helps with planning movement, while its front part takes part in higher thinking such as working memory.
functions: Working memory (holding information in mind briefly)
Contributing to control of eye movements
connections: Supplementary motor area and primary motor cortex
Parietal lobe via long white-matter bundles
clinical: Damage can affect planning, motivation and working memory.
Strokes of the anterior cerebral artery can affect the inner part of this gyrus and cause weakness mainly of the opposite leg.
sfg.lateralization: Present on both sides with broadly similar roles.
sfg.fact: A gyrus is a ridge on the brain surface; the grooves between ridges are called sulci.
sfg.blood_supply: Mainly the anterior cerebral artery; the outer edge is shared with the middle cerebral artery.

mfg.name: Middle frontal gyrus
mfg.tagline: A key area for working memory, attention and directing the eyes.
mfg.overview: The middle frontal gyrus is the middle of the three horizontal ridges on the outer side of the frontal lobe. Much of it forms the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which supports working memory, planning and flexible thinking. Near its back end lies the frontal eye field, which helps move the eyes on purpose.
clinical: Damage can cause difficulty with organising, planning and keeping track of tasks.
Damage to the frontal eye field can briefly make the eyes drift toward the side of the injury.
mfg.lateralization: Both sides contribute; the left is more involved with verbal material and the right with spatial attention in many people.
mfg.fact: The frontal eye fields were among the first brain areas found to move the eyes when stimulated electrically.
mfg.blood_supply: Middle cerebral artery (superior division), with the anterior cerebral artery near the top edge.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

ifg_tri.name: Inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis
ifg_tri.tagline: A triangle-shaped part of Broca's area, important for language.
ifg_tri.overview: The pars triangularis is the middle, triangle-shaped part of the inferior frontal gyrus. Together with the pars opercularis behind it, it forms Broca's area, which in most people is on the left side. It helps select words and their meanings and put sentences together.
connections: Temporal lobe language areas via white-matter bundles
clinical: Damage on the language-dominant side (usually left) can cause Broca-type aphasia: slow, effortful speech with relatively better understanding.
Strokes of the middle cerebral artery are a common cause of damage here.
ifg_tri.lateralization: Language functions are usually on the left. The right side is linked to the tone and rhythm of speech and to holding back actions.
ifg_tri.fact: Broca's area is named after the French physician Paul Broca, who described language loss after frontal damage in 1861.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

ifg_oper.name: Inferior frontal gyrus, pars opercularis
ifg_oper.tagline: The back part of Broca's area, helping plan the movements of speech.
ifg_oper.overview: The pars opercularis is the back part of the inferior frontal gyrus, just in front of the motor areas for the face and mouth. With the pars triangularis it forms Broca's area. It is closely involved in planning the movements needed to speak.
connections: Primary motor cortex for the face and mouth
Temporal and parietal language areas via the arcuate fasciculus
clinical: Damage on the language-dominant side can cause Broca-type aphasia.
Damage can also cause difficulty coordinating speech movements (apraxia of speech).
ifg_oper.lateralization: Language roles are usually on the left. The right side is linked to holding back actions and to the melody of speech.
ifg_oper.fact: 'Opercularis' comes from the Latin for 'lid': this part of the gyrus partly covers the insula like a lid.

precentral.name: Precentral gyrus
precentral.tagline: The main motor strip that sends commands to move the opposite side of the body.
precentral.overview: The precentral gyrus runs from the top of the brain down the side, just in front of the central sulcus. It contains the primary motor cortex, which sends signals down the spinal cord to move muscles. Each part of the body has its own area along the strip, and each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.
functions: Controlling fine finger and hand movements
Controlling face, lips and tongue for speech
Controlling leg movements (on the inner surface)
connections: Spinal cord via the corticospinal tract
Supplementary motor area, basal ganglia and cerebellum via the thalamus
clinical: A stroke here typically causes weakness of the opposite side of the body.
Seizures starting here can cause jerking of one body part that may spread to others.
precentral.lateralization: Each side controls the opposite side of the body.
precentral.fact: The body map along this strip, with large areas for the hands and face, is often drawn as a 'motor homunculus' after the work of Wilder Penfield.
precentral.blood_supply: Middle cerebral artery for the face and arm areas; anterior cerebral artery for the leg area on the inner surface.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

frontal_medial.name: Frontal medial cortex
frontal_medial.tagline: The lower inner frontal lobe, linking feelings with decisions.
frontal_medial.overview: The frontal medial cortex lies on the lower inner surface of the frontal lobe, where the two halves of the brain face each other. It is part of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which helps attach emotional value to choices. It works closely with emotional areas such as the amygdala.
clinical: Damage can change personality and social behaviour while leaving general intelligence largely intact.
Head injuries and some tumours of the skull base can affect this area.
frontal_medial.lateralization: Both sides take part; differences between them are not well established.
frontal_medial.fact: Phineas Gage, a railway worker whose frontal lobe was pierced by an iron rod in 1848, is a famous early case linking this region with personality.
frontal_medial.blood_supply: Anterior cerebral artery (medial orbitofrontal and frontopolar branches).
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

sma.name: Supplementary motor area
sma.tagline: Helps plan and start movements that we decide on ourselves.
sma.overview: The supplementary motor area sits on the inner surface of the frontal lobe, just in front of the leg part of the primary motor cortex. It helps plan sequences of movements and start movements that we choose to make. It also coordinates both sides of the body.
connections: Opposite SMA via the corpus callosum
clinical: Damage can cause reduced spontaneous movement and speech, which often improves over weeks (SMA syndrome).
Seizures from this area can cause unusual postures of both arms.
sma.lateralization: Both sides work together. Speech-related roles lean to the left in most people.
sma.fact: A small electrical signal called the readiness potential can be recorded over this area shortly before a person makes a voluntary movement.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

paracingulate.name: Paracingulate gyrus
paracingulate.tagline: A fold next to the cingulate gyrus that varies a lot between people.
paracingulate.overview: The paracingulate gyrus lies on the inner surface of the frontal lobe, just above the front part of the cingulate gyrus. It is bordered by the paracingulate sulcus, a groove that some brains have and others do not. It takes part in monitoring our own actions and thinking about others.
functions: Thinking about other people's thoughts and intentions
Telling imagined events from real ones
clinical: Damage here usually occurs together with damage to nearby medial frontal areas.
Its fold pattern varies greatly between healthy people, so differences on a scan are usually normal anatomy.
paracingulate.lateralization: The paracingulate sulcus is often more prominent on the left side.
paracingulate.fact: The paracingulate sulcus is present in some brains and absent in others, and often differs between the left and right sides.
sources: Vanderah & Gould, Nolte's The Human Brain 7e (2016)

orbitofrontal.name: Orbitofrontal cortex
orbitofrontal.tagline: The underside of the frontal lobe, involved in reward, smell and social behaviour.
orbitofrontal.overview: The orbitofrontal cortex is the underside of the frontal lobe, resting just above the eye sockets. It helps work out how rewarding or unpleasant something is, and updates this when things change. It also receives information about smell and taste.
clinical: It is commonly bruised in head injuries because it rests on the bony floor of the skull.
Damage may cause impulsive or socially inappropriate behaviour.
Tumours near the base of the skull can press on it.
orbitofrontal.lateralization: Both sides take part; differences between them are not well established.
orbitofrontal.fact: 'Orbito' refers to the orbits, the bony sockets that hold the eyes, which lie directly beneath this area.
orbitofrontal.blood_supply: Anterior cerebral artery (medial part) and middle cerebral artery (lateral part).
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

frontal_operculum.name: Frontal operculum
frontal_operculum.tagline: The frontal 'lid' over the insula, involved in taste and speech.
frontal_operculum.overview: The frontal operculum is the part of the frontal lobe that folds over and covers the front of the insula. It lies deep to Broca's area and is closely linked with it. Together with the front of the insula, it contains the primary taste cortex.
clinical: Damage on the language-dominant side can contribute to speech difficulties.
Damage to both opercula can cause severe difficulty with voluntary face, tongue and swallowing movements.
frontal_operculum.lateralization: Language-related roles are usually on the left; taste is handled on both sides.
frontal_operculum.fact: 'Operculum' means 'little lid' in Latin: the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula together hide the insula from view.

insula.name: Insula
insula.tagline: A hidden lobe that senses the body's inner state, taste and pain.
insula.overview: The insula is a region of cortex folded deep inside the lateral sulcus, hidden under the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes. It receives information about the inside of the body, such as heartbeat, breathing and gut feelings. It combines this with emotion and helps create our sense of how we feel.
functions: Helping regulate heart rate and blood pressure
clinical: It is often involved in strokes of the middle cerebral artery.
Seizures can start in the insula and cause unusual sensations in the throat, chest or stomach.
insula.lateralization: Both sides take part; some studies suggest differences between left and right for bodily and emotional processing.
insula.fact: 'Insula' is Latin for 'island'; it is sometimes called the Island of Reil after the German anatomist Johann Christian Reil.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

temporal_pole.name: Temporal pole
temporal_pole.tagline: The front tip of the temporal lobe, linked to knowledge of words and people.
temporal_pole.overview: The temporal pole is the front tip of each temporal lobe, sitting behind the eye socket. It is thought to bring together information about meaning, such as what objects are and who people are. It is also closely linked with emotional areas.
functions: Knowledge of word and object meanings
connections: Uncinate fasciculus to the frontal lobe
clinical: Shrinkage here is seen in semantic dementia, where people gradually lose the meaning of words.
It is often involved in temporal lobe epilepsy and in head injuries.
temporal_pole.lateralization: The left side is more involved with words and the right with recognising people and emotions, in many people.
temporal_pole.fact: The temporal pole sits in a bony hollow at the base of the skull called the middle cranial fossa.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

stg.name: Superior temporal gyrus
stg.tagline: The top ridge of the temporal lobe, central to hearing and understanding speech.
stg.overview: The superior temporal gyrus is the uppermost ridge of the temporal lobe, running just below the lateral sulcus. It contains areas that process sounds, and its back part on the language-dominant side forms Wernicke's area. This region is central to understanding spoken language.
functions: Perceiving the tone and emotion of speech
connections: Broca's area via the arcuate fasciculus
clinical: Damage to the back part on the language-dominant side can cause Wernicke-type aphasia: fluent speech that may not make sense, with poor understanding.
Strokes of the middle cerebral artery (inferior division) commonly affect this area.
stg.lateralization: Language understanding is usually on the left; the right side is more involved with voice, music and tone of speech.
stg.fact: Wernicke's area is named after the German neurologist Carl Wernicke, who described it in 1874.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

mtg.name: Middle temporal gyrus
mtg.tagline: A ridge on the side of the temporal lobe linked with word meaning.
mtg.overview: The middle temporal gyrus runs along the side of the temporal lobe, between the superior and inferior temporal gyri. It is involved in understanding the meaning of words and in recognising actions. Its back part, near the occipital lobe, contains areas that help us see motion.
functions: Retrieving knowledge about objects and actions
Interpreting other people's movements and gestures
clinical: Damage on the language-dominant side can affect understanding of words.
It can be affected in strokes, tumours and temporal lobe epilepsy.
mtg.lateralization: Word meaning is mainly handled on the left in most people.
mtg.fact: The visual motion area often called MT or V5 sits near where this gyrus meets the occipital lobe.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

itg.name: Inferior temporal gyrus
itg.tagline: The lower temporal ridge, part of the 'what' pathway for recognising objects.
itg.overview: The inferior temporal gyrus forms the lower edge of the side of the temporal lobe. It belongs to the visual 'what' pathway, which identifies objects by their shape. It links what we see with what we know about it.
clinical: Damage, especially on both sides, can impair recognising objects by sight (visual agnosia).
It may be affected by strokes of the posterior or middle cerebral arteries.
itg.lateralization: Both sides take part; the left is more involved with words and the right with faces in many people.
itg.fact: Studies in monkeys found cells in this region that respond to whole objects, such as faces or hands, rather than simple lines.
itg.blood_supply: Middle cerebral artery and posterior cerebral artery (inferior temporal branches).
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

temporal_fusiform.name: Temporal fusiform cortex
temporal_fusiform.tagline: The front part of the fusiform gyrus, helping recognise objects and people.
temporal_fusiform.overview: The temporal fusiform cortex is the front part of the fusiform gyrus, on the underside of the temporal lobe. It is part of the visual recognition pathway and links what we see with stored knowledge. It is involved in recognising objects, faces and their meanings.
clinical: Damage can contribute to difficulty recognising faces (prosopagnosia) or objects.
It is often involved in conditions affecting the base of the temporal lobe.
temporal_fusiform.lateralization: Face recognition leans to the right and word-related processing to the left in many people.
temporal_fusiform.fact: 'Fusiform' means spindle-shaped: the gyrus is wider in the middle and tapers at both ends.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

planum_polare.name: Planum polare
planum_polare.tagline: A flat area in front of the hearing cortex that processes complex sounds.
planum_polare.overview: The planum polare is a flat stretch of cortex on the upper surface of the temporal lobe, in front of Heschl's gyrus. It is hidden inside the lateral sulcus. It is an auditory association area thought to help process complex sounds such as speech and music.
functions: Linking sounds with other temporal lobe areas
clinical: Damage here alone is uncommon; it is usually affected together with nearby auditory areas.
It can be involved in strokes of the middle cerebral artery.
planum_polare.lateralization: Present on both sides; differences between them are not well established.
planum_polare.fact: 'Planum' means 'flat surface' in Latin; 'polare' refers to its position toward the temporal pole.

heschl.name: Heschl's gyrus
heschl.tagline: The primary hearing cortex, where sound first reaches the cortex.
heschl.overview: Heschl's gyrus is a short ridge that runs across the upper surface of the temporal lobe, hidden inside the lateral sulcus. It contains the primary auditory cortex, the first cortical stop for sound information. Different pitches are mapped in an orderly way along it.
functions: Receiving sound signals from the ears
Detecting loudness and timing of sounds
Passing sound information to association areas
connections: Planum temporale and superior temporal gyrus
Opposite auditory cortex via the corpus callosum
clinical: Because each side receives sound from both ears, damage on one side rarely causes deafness.
Damage on both sides is rare but can cause cortical deafness or difficulty recognising sounds.
heschl.lateralization: Present on both sides; each receives input from both ears. Some people have two Heschl's gyri on one side, which is a normal variant.
heschl.fact: It is named after the Austrian anatomist Richard Heschl, who described it in the 19th century.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

planum_temporale.name: Planum temporale
planum_temporale.tagline: A flat area behind the hearing cortex, often larger on the left.
planum_temporale.overview: The planum temporale is a triangular flat area on the upper surface of the temporal lobe, behind Heschl's gyrus. It is an auditory association area involved in processing speech sounds and locating sounds. On the language-dominant side it forms part of Wernicke's area.
connections: Broca's area via the arcuate fasciculus
clinical: Damage on the language-dominant side can contribute to Wernicke-type aphasia.
It can be affected in strokes of the middle cerebral artery.
planum_temporale.lateralization: In many people it is larger on the left, which is thought to relate to language.
planum_temporale.fact: A 1968 study by Geschwind and Levitsky showed that this area is often larger on the left side of the brain.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

postcentral.name: Postcentral gyrus
postcentral.tagline: The main touch strip, feeling the opposite side of the body.
postcentral.overview: The postcentral gyrus runs just behind the central sulcus, parallel to the motor strip. It contains the primary somatosensory cortex, which receives touch, pressure, temperature, pain and body-position signals. Like the motor strip, it holds a map of the body, and each side feels the opposite side.
functions: Sensing the position of body parts
clinical: A stroke here can cause numbness or reduced feeling on the opposite side of the body.
Seizures from this area can cause tingling that may spread across a body part.
postcentral.lateralization: Each side feels the opposite side of the body.
postcentral.fact: Like the motor strip, it contains a body map with large areas for the lips and fingertips, which are very sensitive.
postcentral.blood_supply: Middle cerebral artery for the face and arm areas; anterior cerebral artery for the leg area.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

spl.name: Superior parietal lobule
spl.tagline: Helps us know where things are and guide our hands toward them.
spl.overview: The superior parietal lobule is the upper part of the parietal lobe, behind the touch strip. It combines information from vision and touch to build a sense of where our body and surrounding objects are. This helps guide reaching, grasping and attention in space.
functions: Sensing where the body is in space
connections: Premotor and frontal eye field areas
clinical: Damage can cause difficulty reaching accurately for objects seen (optic ataxia).
Damage on both sides can cause Balint syndrome, with trouble seeing more than one object at a time.
spl.lateralization: Both sides take part; the right side plays a larger role in spatial attention in many people.
spl.fact: This region is part of the visual 'where' or 'how' pathway, which guides actions toward objects.
spl.blood_supply: A border zone between the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

supramarginal.name: Supramarginal gyrus
aka: Part of the inferior parietal lobule
supramarginal.tagline: Involved in speech sounds, skilled movements and body awareness.
supramarginal.overview: The supramarginal gyrus curves around the back end of the lateral sulcus, in the lower parietal lobe. It helps process the sounds of words and supports skilled movements such as using tools. It also contributes to awareness of our body and touch.
functions: Planning skilled movements such as using tools
connections: Superior temporal gyrus and planum temporale
Broca's area via the arcuate fasciculus
clinical: Damage on the left can cause difficulty performing skilled movements on request (apraxia).
Damage can cause conduction aphasia, with particular difficulty repeating words.
supramarginal.lateralization: Language and skilled movement roles are usually on the left; the right side is more involved in spatial attention.
supramarginal.fact: 'Supramarginal' means 'above the margin': it arches over the end of the lateral sulcus.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

angular.name: Angular gyrus
aka: Part of the inferior parietal lobule
angular.tagline: A crossroads area linked with reading, writing, numbers and meaning.
angular.overview: The angular gyrus lies at the back of the lower parietal lobe, where the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes meet. It brings together information from different senses. It is involved in reading, writing, working with numbers and understanding meaning.
functions: Understanding the meaning of words and sentences
connections: Visual areas in the occipital lobe
clinical: Damage on the left can cause Gerstmann syndrome: trouble with writing, calculation, naming fingers and telling left from right.
Damage can also cause loss of reading and writing ability.
angular.lateralization: Language and number roles are usually on the left; the right side is more involved with spatial attention.
angular.fact: In 1891 the French neurologist Jules Dejerine linked damage here with a loss of both reading and writing.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

precuneus.name: Precuneus
precuneus.tagline: An inner parietal area involved in memory, imagination and self-reflection.
precuneus.overview: The precuneus is on the inner surface of the parietal lobe, in front of the cuneus. It is a key part of the default mode network, which is active when we are not focused on the outside world. It is involved in recalling personal memories, mental imagery and thinking about ourselves.
clinical: Reduced activity here and in the posterior cingulate is often seen early in Alzheimer's disease on functional scans.
Isolated damage here is uncommon.
precuneus.fact: 'Precuneus' means 'in front of the cuneus', the wedge-shaped area of the occipital lobe.
precuneus.blood_supply: Anterior cerebral artery, with the posterior cerebral artery supplying its back part.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

parietal_operculum.name: Parietal operculum
parietal_operculum.tagline: The parietal 'lid' over the insula, a second-stage area for touch.
parietal_operculum.overview: The parietal operculum is the part of the parietal lobe that folds over the back of the insula. It contains the secondary somatosensory cortex, which further processes touch and pain. It receives information from both sides of the body.
functions: Combining sensations from both sides of the body
clinical: Damage can affect recognising objects by touch.
It is involved in some pain-related conditions after stroke.
parietal_operculum.lateralization: Present on both sides; each receives input from both sides of the body.
parietal_operculum.fact: Unlike the primary touch strip, this area responds to touch on both sides of the body.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

central_operculum.name: Central operculum
central_operculum.tagline: The lower ends of the motor and touch strips, serving the mouth and throat.
central_operculum.overview: The central operculum is where the lower ends of the precentral and postcentral gyri fold over the insula. It contains the motor and sensory areas for the face, tongue, mouth and throat. It is important for speaking, chewing and swallowing.
functions: Feeling in the mouth and face
Contributing to speech articulation and taste
connections: Brainstem nuclei for the face and throat
clinical: Damage on one side can cause mild weakness of the lower face on the opposite side.
Damage on both sides can cause severe difficulty with voluntary speaking and swallowing.
central_operculum.lateralization: Each side mainly controls the opposite lower face, although throat muscles receive input from both sides.
central_operculum.fact: The mouth and tongue have unusually large areas on the motor and touch maps, reflecting their fine control and sensitivity.

lateral_occipital.name: Lateral occipital cortex
lateral_occipital.tagline: The outer back of the brain, where vision builds up shapes and objects.
lateral_occipital.overview: The lateral occipital cortex covers the outer surface of the occipital lobe. It is a visual association area that receives signals from the primary visual cortex. It helps recognise object shapes and, near the temporal lobe, contributes to seeing motion.
functions: Passing visual information forward to temporal and parietal lobes
clinical: Damage can cause difficulty recognising objects by sight (visual agnosia).
Rarely, damage near the motion area can impair seeing movement.
lateral_occipital.lateralization: Present on both sides with similar roles.
lateral_occipital.fact: 'Extrastriate' means 'outside the striate cortex', the striped primary visual area.
lateral_occipital.blood_supply: Posterior cerebral artery, with middle cerebral artery branches on the outer surface.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

intracalcarine.name: Intracalcarine cortex
intracalcarine.tagline: The primary visual cortex, lining the calcarine sulcus.
intracalcarine.overview: The intracalcarine cortex lines the calcarine sulcus, a deep groove on the inner surface of the occipital lobe. It contains the primary visual cortex, the first cortical stop for signals from the eyes. Each side sees the opposite half of the visual world.
functions: Passing visual information to higher areas
connections: Thalamus (lateral geniculate nucleus) via the optic radiation
clinical: Damage causes loss of vision in the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes (homonymous hemianopia).
Strokes of the posterior cerebral artery are a common cause.
intracalcarine.lateralization: Each side sees the opposite half of the visual world.
intracalcarine.fact: A pale stripe of fibres, the stria of Gennari, is visible here to the naked eye, giving it the name 'striate cortex'.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

supracalcarine.name: Supracalcarine cortex
aka: Upper bank of the calcarine sulcus
supracalcarine.tagline: Visual cortex above the calcarine groove, seeing the lower field of view.
supracalcarine.overview: The supracalcarine cortex lies just above the calcarine sulcus on the inner surface of the occipital lobe. Like the cortex inside the sulcus, it handles early visual processing. Areas above the calcarine sulcus represent the lower part of the opposite visual field.
functions: Passing signals to higher visual areas
clinical: Damage can cause loss of vision in the lower quarter of the opposite visual field.
Strokes of the posterior cerebral artery are a common cause.
supracalcarine.lateralization: Each side sees the opposite half of the visual world.
supracalcarine.fact: The visual map is flipped: the upper bank of the calcarine sulcus sees the lower part of the world.

cuneus.name: Cuneus
cuneus.tagline: A wedge of visual cortex on the inner back of the brain.
cuneus.overview: The cuneus is a wedge-shaped area on the inner surface of the occipital lobe, between the calcarine sulcus and the parieto-occipital sulcus. It contains visual cortex that represents the lower part of the opposite visual field. It passes signals on to higher visual areas.
functions: Passing visual information to parietal areas
connections: Lateral geniculate nucleus via the optic radiation
clinical: Damage can cause loss of vision in the lower quarter of the opposite visual field.
It may be affected in strokes of the posterior cerebral artery.
cuneus.lateralization: Each side sees the opposite half of the visual world.
cuneus.fact: 'Cuneus' is Latin for 'wedge', describing its shape.
cuneus.blood_supply: Posterior cerebral artery (calcarine and parieto-occipital branches).

lingual.name: Lingual gyrus
lingual.tagline: Visual cortex below the calcarine groove, involved in colour and the upper field.
lingual.overview: The lingual gyrus lies below the calcarine sulcus on the inner and lower surface of the occipital lobe. It represents the upper part of the opposite visual field. It also contributes to processing colour and recognising places.
clinical: Damage can cause loss of vision in the upper quarter of the opposite visual field.
Damage to this area and the nearby fusiform gyrus can impair colour vision (achromatopsia).
lingual.lateralization: Each side sees the opposite half of the visual world.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

occipital_fusiform.name: Occipital fusiform gyrus
occipital_fusiform.tagline: The back of the fusiform gyrus, involved in colour and object vision.
occipital_fusiform.overview: The occipital fusiform gyrus is the back part of the fusiform gyrus, on the underside of the occipital lobe. It belongs to the visual 'what' pathway. It helps process colour and the shapes of objects before information moves forward into the temporal lobe.
functions: Early steps in recognising faces and words
Passing visual information to temporal areas
clinical: Damage can impair colour perception (achromatopsia).
It may be affected by strokes of the posterior cerebral artery, often with an upper visual field loss.
occipital_fusiform.lateralization: Present on both sides with broadly similar roles.
occipital_fusiform.fact: A person with damage to this region on both sides may see the world in shades of grey.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

temporo_occipital_fusiform.name: Temporal occipital fusiform cortex
temporo_occipital_fusiform.tagline: Where the brain specialises in recognising faces and written words.
temporo_occipital_fusiform.overview: This region is the middle part of the fusiform gyrus, where the occipital and temporal lobes meet on the underside of the brain. It contains areas that respond strongly to faces and, usually on the left, to written words. It is a key step in the visual 'what' pathway.
clinical: Damage, more often on the right, can cause face blindness (prosopagnosia).
Damage on the left can cause pure alexia, a loss of reading with preserved writing.
temporo_occipital_fusiform.lateralization: Face recognition leans to the right and word recognition to the left in most people.
temporo_occipital_fusiform.fact: Some people are born with difficulty recognising faces even though their brain scans look normal.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

occipital_pole.name: Occipital pole
occipital_pole.tagline: The very back tip of the brain, handling sharp central vision.
occipital_pole.overview: The occipital pole is the rearmost tip of each hemisphere. It contains the part of the visual cortex that processes the centre of our vision, where we see detail most sharply. A large share of visual cortex is devoted to this small central area.
functions: Reading fine print and seeing detail
Passing signals to higher visual areas
clinical: Damage can cause loss of central vision on the opposite side.
It can be injured when the back of the head is hit.
occipital_pole.lateralization: Each side handles the opposite half of central vision.
occipital_pole.fact: This tip lies where the posterior and middle cerebral artery territories meet, which may help explain why central vision is sometimes spared in strokes.
occipital_pole.blood_supply: Posterior cerebral artery, with a contribution from the middle cerebral artery in some people.

cingulate_ant.name: Anterior cingulate cortex
cingulate_ant.tagline: Monitors conflicts and errors and links emotion with action.
cingulate_ant.overview: The anterior cingulate cortex is the front part of the cingulate gyrus, which curves around the front of the corpus callosum. It helps notice errors and conflicts and adjusts our behaviour. It also contributes to emotion, motivation and how unpleasant pain feels.
clinical: Damage on both sides can cause severe lack of motivation and spontaneous movement (akinetic mutism).
It is studied in research on mood disorders and chronic pain.
cingulate_ant.fact: 'Cingulate' comes from the Latin for 'belt' or 'girdle', as this gyrus wraps around the corpus callosum.
cingulate_ant.blood_supply: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal and callosomarginal branches).
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

cingulate_post.name: Posterior cingulate cortex
cingulate_post.tagline: A hub of the brain's 'resting' network, linked with memory and self-reflection.
cingulate_post.overview: The posterior cingulate cortex is the back part of the cingulate gyrus, curving over the corpus callosum. It is a central hub of the default mode network, which is active during daydreaming and recalling memories. It also helps with orientation and finding our way.
functions: Shifting between inward and outward attention
clinical: Reduced activity here is often seen early in Alzheimer's disease on functional scans.
Damage to the nearby retrosplenial area can cause trouble finding one's way.
cingulate_post.fact: This is one of the most active regions of the brain when a person is resting and not focused on a task.
cingulate_post.blood_supply: Anterior cerebral artery, with the posterior cerebral artery supplying the back part.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

subcallosal.name: Subcallosal cortex
subcallosal.tagline: A small area below the corpus callosum linked with mood and body regulation.
subcallosal.overview: The subcallosal cortex is a small area on the inner surface of the frontal lobe, just below the front end of the corpus callosum. It is part of the limbic system. It is involved in mood and in linking emotions with body responses such as heart rate.
clinical: It is studied in research on depression.
It has been investigated experimentally as a target for deep brain stimulation in severe depression.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)
Vanderah & Gould, Nolte's The Human Brain 7e (2016)

parahippocampal.name: Parahippocampal gyrus
parahippocampal.tagline: The gateway between the hippocampus and the rest of the cortex.
parahippocampal.overview: The parahippocampal gyrus lies on the inner underside of the temporal lobe, next to the hippocampus. Its front part, the entorhinal cortex, is the main gateway for information entering and leaving the hippocampus. Its back part helps recognise places and scenes.
functions: Passing information to and from the hippocampus
clinical: The entorhinal cortex is among the first areas affected in Alzheimer's disease.
Damage can cause difficulty forming new memories or finding one's way.
parahippocampal.lateralization: Both sides work together; the left leans toward verbal and the right toward spatial memory in many people.
parahippocampal.fact: The front of this gyrus hooks back on itself to form the uncus, which can press on brainstem structures when the brain is swollen.
parahippocampal.blood_supply: Posterior cerebral artery, with the anterior choroidal artery at the front.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

hippocampus.name: Hippocampus
hippocampus.tagline: Essential for forming new memories and finding our way.
hippocampus.overview: The hippocampus is a curved structure tucked inside each temporal lobe, along the floor of the lateral ventricle. It is essential for turning new experiences into lasting memories. It also helps build mental maps of places.
functions: Forming new memories of facts and events
Linking details into a single memory
connections: Mammillary bodies and thalamus via the fornix
clinical: It shrinks in Alzheimer's disease and can be measured on MRI.
Scarring here (hippocampal sclerosis) is a common cause of temporal lobe epilepsy.
It is sensitive to lack of oxygen.
hippocampus.lateralization: The left is more involved with verbal memory and the right with spatial memory in many people.
hippocampus.fact: Its name comes from the Greek for 'seahorse', which its shape resembles. 'Place cells' discovered here earned a Nobel Prize in 2014.
hippocampus.blood_supply: Posterior cerebral artery (hippocampal branches) and the anterior choroidal artery.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

amygdala.name: Amygdala
amygdala.tagline: An almond-shaped cluster that detects threats and tags memories with emotion.
amygdala.overview: The amygdala is a group of nuclei deep in the front of each temporal lobe, just in front of the hippocampus. It helps detect threats and other emotionally important events. It also strengthens memories of emotional experiences and helps read social signals such as facial expressions.
functions: Detecting threats and triggering fear responses
Learning which things are rewarding or dangerous
clinical: Seizures from the temporal lobe often involve the amygdala and may begin with a sudden feeling of fear.
Rare damage on both sides can impair recognising fear in others.
amygdala.lateralization: Both sides take part; differences between left and right are debated.
amygdala.fact: 'Amygdala' is Greek for 'almond', describing its shape.
amygdala.blood_supply: Anterior choroidal artery and branches of the middle cerebral artery.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

thalamus.name: Thalamus
thalamus.tagline: The brain's relay hub, passing sensory and motor signals to the cortex.
thalamus.overview: The thalamus is a pair of egg-shaped grey-matter masses in the centre of the brain, on either side of the third ventricle. Almost all sensory information, except smell, passes through it on the way to the cortex. It also relays motor signals and helps regulate alertness and attention.
functions: Relaying sight, hearing, touch and taste to the cortex
Relaying signals from the cerebellum and basal ganglia
connections: Almost every area of the cerebral cortex
Spinal cord and brainstem sensory pathways
Hippocampal circuit via the mammillary bodies
clinical: A thalamic stroke can cause numbness on the opposite side of the body.
Some people develop persistent pain after a thalamic stroke (thalamic pain syndrome).
Damage to certain thalamic nuclei can affect memory or alertness.
thalamus.lateralization: Each side mainly serves the opposite side of the body.
thalamus.fact: 'Thalamus' comes from the Greek for 'inner chamber'.
thalamus.blood_supply: Small perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and posterior communicating arteries, plus the posterior choroidal arteries.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

caudate.name: Caudate nucleus
caudate.tagline: A C-shaped nucleus of the basal ganglia, involved in learning and goals.
caudate.overview: The caudate nucleus is a C-shaped structure that curves alongside the lateral ventricle, with a large head at the front and a thin tail. It is part of the basal ganglia and, with the putamen, forms the striatum. It helps with goal-directed behaviour, learning and controlling movement.
clinical: It shrinks in Huntington's disease, making the front horns of the lateral ventricles look larger.
It can be affected by small strokes from deep perforating arteries.
caudate.lateralization: Present on both sides with similar roles.
caudate.fact: 'Caudate' means 'having a tail', describing its long curved tail.
caudate.blood_supply: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery and the recurrent artery of Heubner from the anterior cerebral artery.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

putamen.name: Putamen
putamen.tagline: A basal ganglia nucleus that helps control and learn movements.
putamen.overview: The putamen is a rounded structure deep in each hemisphere, on the outer side of the globus pallidus. With the caudate nucleus it forms the striatum, the main input station of the basal ganglia. It helps control movement and form motor habits.
clinical: In Parkinson's disease, loss of dopamine input to the putamen causes slowness and stiffness.
It is a common site of bleeding in people with long-standing high blood pressure.
putamen.lateralization: Each side mainly helps control the opposite side of the body.
putamen.fact: 'Putamen' comes from the Latin for 'shell' or 'husk'.
putamen.blood_supply: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

pallidum.name: Globus pallidus
pallidum.tagline: The main output station of the basal ganglia, fine-tuning movement.
pallidum.overview: The globus pallidus sits just inside the putamen, deep in each hemisphere. It has an outer and an inner part; the inner part is a main output of the basal ganglia. It sends signals to the thalamus that help allow wanted movements and suppress unwanted ones.
functions: Sending basal ganglia output to the thalamus
clinical: The inner part is a target for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease and dystonia.
Both sides can be damaged by carbon monoxide poisoning.
pallidum.lateralization: Each side mainly helps control the opposite side of the body.
pallidum.fact: 'Pallidus' means 'pale': it looks paler than nearby grey matter because of its many myelinated fibres.
pallidum.blood_supply: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery and the anterior choroidal artery.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

accumbens.name: Nucleus accumbens
accumbens.tagline: A small hub for reward, motivation and learning what feels good.
accumbens.overview: The nucleus accumbens is a small area where the caudate and putamen meet at the front, near the base of the brain. It is the main part of the ventral striatum. It receives dopamine signals and helps link reward with motivation and action.
clinical: It is a major focus of research on addiction.
It is studied in research on depression and loss of pleasure.
accumbens.lateralization: Present on both sides with similar roles.
accumbens.fact: Its full name, nucleus accumbens septi, means 'nucleus leaning against the septum'.
accumbens.blood_supply: Recurrent artery of Heubner and medial lenticulostriate arteries.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

ventral_dc.name: Ventral diencephalon
ventral_dc.tagline: A label grouping the hypothalamus and nearby deep structures.
ventral_dc.overview: Ventral diencephalon is a label used by brain-mapping software for a group of small structures below the thalamus that are hard to separate on MRI. It includes the hypothalamus, the mammillary bodies, the subthalamic nucleus and parts of the substantia nigra, plus nearby fibres. Together these help control hormones, body balance and movement.
functions: Regulating hormones via the pituitary gland (hypothalamus)
Controlling body temperature, hunger and thirst
clinical: The subthalamic nucleus is a common target for deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.
The mammillary bodies can be damaged by severe thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, affecting memory.
Tumours near the pituitary can affect the hypothalamus.
ventral_dc.lateralization: Present on both sides around the third ventricle.
ventral_dc.fact: This is a software label rather than a single anatomical structure; it bundles several tiny regions that MRI cannot easily tell apart.
ventral_dc.blood_supply: Small perforating branches from the circle of Willis, including the posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

lateral_ventricle.name: Lateral ventricle
lateral_ventricle.tagline: The largest fluid-filled spaces inside the brain, one in each hemisphere.
lateral_ventricle.overview: The lateral ventricles are two C-shaped cavities, one in each hemisphere, filled with cerebrospinal fluid. Each has a body and horns that reach into the frontal, temporal and occipital lobes. They contain choroid plexus tissue, which produces much of the brain's fluid.
functions: Producing fluid via the choroid plexus
connections: Third ventricle via the interventricular foramina (of Monro)
Caudate nucleus and thalamus along its walls
Hippocampus along the temporal horn floor
clinical: They enlarge when fluid flow is blocked (hydrocephalus).
They often become larger with age as surrounding brain tissue shrinks.
Mild differences in size between left and right are common and usually normal.
lateral_ventricle.lateralization: One in each hemisphere; slight asymmetry is common.
lateral_ventricle.fact: The brain makes roughly half a litre of cerebrospinal fluid a day, so the fluid is replaced several times daily.
lateral_ventricle.blood_supply: Choroid plexus fed by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.

third_ventricle.name: Third ventricle
third_ventricle.tagline: A narrow midline fluid space between the two halves of the thalamus.
third_ventricle.overview: The third ventricle is a narrow, slit-like cavity in the midline of the brain, between the left and right thalamus. It receives fluid from the lateral ventricles and passes it down through a small channel called the cerebral aqueduct. The hypothalamus forms part of its walls and floor.
functions: Passing cerebrospinal fluid from the lateral ventricles
Producing fluid via its choroid plexus
Connecting to the fourth ventricle via the cerebral aqueduct
connections: Lateral ventricles via the interventricular foramina
Fourth ventricle via the cerebral aqueduct
Thalamus and hypothalamus in its walls
clinical: A blockage at its entry or exit can cause hydrocephalus.
Narrowing of the cerebral aqueduct is a known cause of hydrocephalus.
third_ventricle.fact: The cerebral aqueduct that drains it is only a few millimetres wide, making it a common site of blockage.
third_ventricle.blood_supply: Choroid plexus fed by the medial posterior choroidal arteries.

fourth_ventricle.name: Fourth ventricle
fourth_ventricle.tagline: A tent-shaped fluid space between the brainstem and the cerebellum.
fourth_ventricle.overview: The fourth ventricle is a diamond- or tent-shaped cavity lying behind the pons and upper medulla and in front of the cerebellum. It receives fluid from the cerebral aqueduct. Small openings let the fluid leave the ventricles and flow around the brain and spinal cord.
functions: Passing fluid out of the ventricle system
Producing fluid via its choroid plexus
Connecting to the central canal of the spinal cord
Bordering important brainstem nuclei on its floor
connections: Cerebral aqueduct from the third ventricle
Subarachnoid space via the foramina of Luschka and Magendie
Pons, medulla and cerebellum around it
clinical: Tumours in the back of the head (posterior fossa) can block it and cause hydrocephalus.
Its shape is changed by swelling or bleeding in the cerebellum.
fourth_ventricle.fact: Its floor, the rhomboid fossa, contains nuclei that control many cranial nerves, such as those for eye movement, facial movement and swallowing.
fourth_ventricle.blood_supply: Choroid plexus fed by branches of the posterior and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries.

corpus_callosum.name: Corpus callosum
corpus_callosum.tagline: The thick bridge of fibres connecting the left and right hemispheres.
corpus_callosum.overview: The corpus callosum is a broad, arched band of white matter that joins the two cerebral hemispheres. It contains a very large number of nerve fibres that let both sides share information. It has a front part (genu), a middle part (body) and a thick back part (splenium).
functions: Combining sight and touch from both sides
Supporting language and attention across hemispheres
connections: Matching areas of the left and right cortex
Occipital and parietal lobes (via the splenium)
clinical: It can be affected in multiple sclerosis.
Surgically cutting part of it (callosotomy) is sometimes used for severe epilepsy.
It may be partly or completely absent from birth, sometimes with few symptoms.
corpus_callosum.lateralization: Single midline structure joining both hemispheres.
corpus_callosum.fact: Studies of 'split-brain' patients, whose corpus callosum had been cut, earned Roger Sperry a Nobel Prize in 1981.
corpus_callosum.blood_supply: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal branches); the splenium also from the posterior cerebral artery.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

cerebral_white_matter.name: Cerebral white matter
cerebral_white_matter.tagline: The brain's wiring: bundles of insulated nerve fibres linking regions.
cerebral_white_matter.overview: Cerebral white matter lies beneath the cortex and is made of nerve fibres wrapped in a fatty insulation called myelin. These fibres connect areas within a hemisphere, link the two hemispheres, and carry signals to and from the brainstem and spinal cord. Its pale colour comes from the myelin.
functions: Carrying signals to and from the spinal cord
Speeding up nerve signals through myelin insulation
connections: All areas of the cerebral cortex
Thalamus and basal ganglia via the internal capsule
clinical: Multiple sclerosis causes patches of damage in white matter.
Small bright spots on FLAIR or T2 scans become more common with age and are often linked to small-vessel disease; their meaning must be judged by a doctor.
cerebral_white_matter.fact: Myelin is mostly made of fat, which is why white matter looks pale in fresh brain tissue.
cerebral_white_matter.blood_supply: Long penetrating branches of the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)
Osborn's Brain: Imaging, Pathology, and Anatomy 2e

cerebellum_hemi.name: Cerebellar hemisphere
cerebellum_hemi.tagline: Coordinates smooth, accurate movements of the limbs on the same side.
cerebellum_hemi.overview: The cerebellar hemispheres are the two large side portions of the cerebellum, at the back of the head below the cerebrum. Their tightly folded cortex compares intended movements with actual ones and corrects them. They also contribute to timing, motor learning and some thinking skills.
functions: Contributing to some thinking and language tasks
connections: Cerebral cortex via the pons and thalamus
clinical: Damage causes clumsiness and poor coordination on the same side of the body.
Strokes or bleeding here can cause dizziness, vomiting and unsteadiness.
cerebellum_hemi.lateralization: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls the same side of the body.
cerebellum_hemi.fact: The cerebellum contains more than half of all the neurons in the brain, mostly tiny granule cells.
cerebellum_hemi.blood_supply: Superior cerebellar, anterior inferior cerebellar and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

cerebellar_vermis.name: Cerebellar vermis
cerebellar_vermis.tagline: The middle strip of the cerebellum, controlling balance and posture.
cerebellar_vermis.overview: The vermis is the narrow middle part of the cerebellum, joining the two hemispheres. It helps control posture, balance and walking, and works with the inner ear's balance system. It also helps control eye movements.
clinical: Damage causes unsteady, wide-based walking.
Long-term heavy alcohol use can damage the front part of the vermis.
cerebellar_vermis.fact: 'Vermis' is Latin for 'worm', describing its segmented appearance.
cerebellar_vermis.blood_supply: Superior cerebellar artery (upper part) and posterior inferior cerebellar artery (lower part).

cerebellum_white_matter.name: Cerebellar white matter
cerebellum_white_matter.tagline: The branching core of the cerebellum, containing its deep output nuclei.
cerebellum_white_matter.overview: Cerebellar white matter is the core of the cerebellum, made of nerve fibres running to and from the cerebellar cortex. In a cut section it branches like a tree. The deep cerebellar nuclei, which send the cerebellum's output, are embedded within it.
functions: Carrying signals into the cerebellar cortex
Carrying output from the cortex to the deep nuclei
Linking the cerebellum to the brainstem
connections: Deep cerebellar nuclei, such as the dentate nucleus
clinical: It can be affected in multiple sclerosis.
Damage can cause poor coordination and tremor.
cerebellum_white_matter.fact: Its tree-like pattern is called the arbor vitae, Latin for 'tree of life'.
cerebellum_white_matter.blood_supply: Branches of the superior, anterior inferior and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries.

midbrain.name: Midbrain
midbrain.tagline: The top of the brainstem, controlling eye movements and reflexes.
midbrain.overview: The midbrain is the uppermost part of the brainstem, just below the thalamus. It contains nuclei for eye movement, the substantia nigra, which produces dopamine, and relay centres for vision and hearing reflexes. Large bundles of motor fibres pass through it on the way down.
functions: Controlling eye movements and pupil size
clinical: In Parkinson's disease, dopamine-producing cells of the substantia nigra are lost.
Damage can cause double vision or problems moving the eyes.
Small strokes here can affect eye movements and cause weakness on the opposite side.
midbrain.lateralization: Paired left and right halves around the midline.
midbrain.fact: Its two upper bumps (superior colliculi) help turn the eyes toward sudden movement; the lower two (inferior colliculi) relay hearing.
midbrain.blood_supply: Posterior cerebral artery, superior cerebellar artery and the top of the basilar artery.

pons.name: Pons
pons.tagline: The bulging middle of the brainstem, a bridge to the cerebellum.
pons.overview: The pons is the rounded middle part of the brainstem, between the midbrain and the medulla. Its front part relays signals from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum. It also contains nuclei for facial movement and feeling, eye movement and hearing, and helps regulate breathing and sleep.
functions: Relaying signals between the cortex and cerebellum
connections: Cerebellum via the middle cerebellar peduncles
clinical: A stroke in the front of the pons can cause locked-in syndrome, where a person is awake but almost fully paralysed.
Very rapid correction of low blood sodium can damage the pons (osmotic demyelination).
pons.lateralization: Paired left and right halves around the midline.
pons.blood_supply: Pontine branches of the basilar artery, plus the anterior inferior and superior cerebellar arteries.

medulla.name: Medulla oblongata
medulla.tagline: The lowest part of the brainstem, controlling breathing and heart rate.
medulla.overview: The medulla is the lowest part of the brainstem, continuous with the spinal cord. It contains centres that control breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, and reflexes such as swallowing and coughing. Most motor fibres cross to the opposite side here.
functions: Regulating heart rate and blood pressure
connections: Cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncles
clinical: A stroke on its side (lateral medullary or Wallenberg syndrome) can cause dizziness, swallowing difficulty and altered sensation.
Pressure on the medulla from brain swelling can be life-threatening.
medulla.lateralization: Motor pathways cross here, which is why each half of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.
medulla.blood_supply: Vertebral arteries, the anterior spinal artery and the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries.

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.tagline: The stalk joining brain and spinal cord, running vital body functions.
brainstem.overview: The brainstem connects the cerebrum and cerebellum to the spinal cord and is made of the midbrain, pons and medulla. It carries all signals passing between the brain and body. It also contains centres for breathing, heart rate, alertness and most cranial nerves.
functions: Controlling breathing, heart rate and blood pressure
Eye, face and swallowing control through the cranial nerves
Carrying all motor and sensory pathways
clinical: Brainstem strokes can cause dizziness, double vision, swallowing difficulty and weakness.
Pressure on the brainstem from swelling above it is a medical emergency.
brainstem.lateralization: Paired left and right halves around the midline.
brainstem.fact: Ten of the twelve pairs of cranial nerves attach to the brainstem.
brainstem.blood_supply: Vertebral and basilar arteries and their branches.

cerebral_arteries.name: Cerebral arteries
cerebral_arteries.tagline: The arteries inside the skull, joined at the base by the circle of Willis.
cerebral_arteries.overview: The brain is supplied by two internal carotid arteries at the front and two vertebral arteries at the back. At the base of the brain these join in a ring called the circle of Willis, from which the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries branch out. Each main artery supplies its own territory of brain.
functions: Delivering oxygen and glucose to the brain
Providing back-up routes through the circle of Willis
Supplying deep structures through small perforating branches
Adjusting blood flow to match brain activity
clinical: Blockage of an artery causes an ischaemic stroke in its territory.
Aneurysms (bulges in an artery wall) often form at branch points of the circle of Willis.
Many people have a circle that differs from the textbook diagram; this is usually a normal variant.
cerebral_arteries.lateralization: Paired left and right arteries, joined by communicating arteries.
cerebral_arteries.fact: The brain makes up about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of the body's oxygen at rest.
cerebral_arteries.blood_supply: Fed by the internal carotid and vertebral arteries.
sources: Osborn's Brain: Imaging, Pathology, and Anatomy 2e

neck_arteries.name: Neck arteries
neck_arteries.tagline: The carotid and vertebral arteries that carry blood up the neck to the brain.
neck_arteries.overview: Blood reaches the brain through four arteries in the neck: two carotid arteries at the front and two vertebral arteries at the back. Each common carotid artery divides into an internal branch, which goes to the brain and eye, and an external branch, which supplies the face and scalp. The vertebral arteries run up through holes in the neck bones.
functions: Carrying blood from the heart to the brain
Supplying the face, scalp and neck (external carotid)
connections: Branches to the face and scalp
clinical: Fatty narrowing (atherosclerosis) of the carotid artery can lead to stroke.
A tear in an artery wall (dissection) is a cause of stroke in younger people.
The two vertebral arteries are often unequal in size, which is usually normal.
neck_arteries.lateralization: Paired left and right; the left common carotid usually arises straight from the aorta, the right from the brachiocephalic trunk.
neck_arteries.fact: Pressure sensors in the carotid sinus help the body adjust blood pressure from moment to moment.
neck_arteries.blood_supply: Arise from the aortic arch and its branches.
sources: Osborn's Brain: Imaging, Pathology, and Anatomy 2e

frontal.name: Frontal lobe
frontal.tagline: The front of the brain: planning, decisions, movement and speech.
frontal.overview: The frontal lobe is the largest lobe, lying behind the forehead and in front of the central sulcus. Its back part controls movement, and its front part, the prefrontal cortex, supports planning, judgement, self-control and personality. On the language-dominant side it also contains Broca's area for speech production.
clinical: Damage can cause weakness on the opposite side, speech difficulty or changes in behaviour.
It is commonly affected in head injuries.
frontal.fact: The frontal lobes make up roughly a third of the cerebral cortex in humans.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

parietal.name: Parietal lobe
parietal.tagline: Touch, body awareness and knowing where things are.
parietal.overview: The parietal lobe lies behind the central sulcus, under the crown of the head. Its front strip receives touch and body-position signals, and the areas behind combine touch, vision and hearing. It helps us know where our body and objects are, and supports reading, writing and numbers.
clinical: Damage on the right can cause people to ignore the left side of space (neglect).
Damage on the left can affect language, reading, writing and calculation.
parietal.fact: 'Parietal' comes from the Latin for 'wall', after the parietal bones of the skull above it.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

temporal.name: Temporal lobe
temporal.tagline: Hearing, language understanding, memory and recognising things.
temporal.overview: The temporal lobe lies on the side of the brain, below the lateral sulcus and near the temples. It contains the hearing cortex and, on the language-dominant side, Wernicke's area for understanding speech. Its lower and inner parts help recognise objects and faces and work with the hippocampus to form memories.
clinical: Temporal lobe epilepsy is the most common type of focal epilepsy in adults.
Damage on the language-dominant side can impair understanding of speech.
temporal.fact: The hippocampus and amygdala, key structures for memory and emotion, lie folded inside the inner part of the temporal lobe.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

occipital.name: Occipital lobe
occipital.tagline: The back of the brain, dedicated mainly to vision.
occipital.overview: The occipital lobe is the rearmost lobe, at the back of the head. It contains the primary visual cortex and surrounding areas that process shape, colour and motion. Each side processes the opposite half of what we see.
functions: Receiving visual signals from the eyes
Passing visual information to other lobes
clinical: Damage on one side causes loss of the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes.
Strokes of the posterior cerebral artery are a common cause of occipital damage.
occipital.fact: 'Occipital' comes from the Latin occiput, meaning the back of the head.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

insular.name: Insular lobe
insular.tagline: A hidden lobe that senses the body's inner state.
insular.overview: The insula is a lobe of cortex hidden deep in the lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula. It brings together signals from inside the body with taste, pain and emotion. It is sometimes counted as part of the limbic system.
functions: Awareness of the body's internal state
Regulating heart rate and blood pressure
clinical: It is often affected in middle cerebral artery strokes.
Seizures can start in the insula.
insular.fact: The insula can only be seen when the overlying opercula are pulled apart.

limbic.name: Limbic lobe
limbic.tagline: A ring of structures for emotion, motivation and memory.
limbic.overview: The limbic lobe is a ring of cortex on the inner surface of each hemisphere, curving around the corpus callosum and brainstem. It includes the cingulate and parahippocampal gyri, and is closely tied to the hippocampus and amygdala. Together these form much of the limbic system, which supports emotion, motivation and memory.
clinical: Alzheimer's disease often first affects the hippocampus and nearby areas.
Many temporal lobe seizures start in limbic structures.
limbic.fact: 'Limbic' comes from the Latin limbus, meaning 'border', because it forms a border around the brainstem; the term was used by Paul Broca.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

subcortical.name: Deep grey matter
subcortical.tagline: Deep nuclei that relay signals and shape movement and motivation.
subcortical.overview: Deep grey matter is a set of nuclei buried inside the hemispheres beneath the cortex. It includes the thalamus, which relays information to the cortex, and the basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus and nucleus accumbens), which help select movements and drive motivation. The hypothalamus, which controls hormones and body balance, also lies here.
clinical: Parkinson's and Huntington's diseases affect the basal ganglia.
Small deep strokes and bleeds often affect these structures.
subcortical.fact: The basal ganglia work in loops: signals leave the cortex, pass through these nuclei and the thalamus, and return to the cortex.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

ventricles.name: Ventricles
ventricles.tagline: Fluid-filled spaces inside the brain that make and carry cerebrospinal fluid.
ventricles.overview: The ventricles are four connected cavities inside the brain: two lateral ventricles, the third ventricle and the fourth ventricle. They contain cerebrospinal fluid, which is made mainly by the choroid plexus. The fluid flows out of the fourth ventricle to surround the brain and spinal cord.
clinical: Blocked fluid flow causes the ventricles to enlarge (hydrocephalus).
The ventricles naturally become larger with age.
ventricles.fact: The total volume of cerebrospinal fluid in an adult is about 150 millilitres.

white_matter.name: White matter
white_matter.tagline: The brain's wiring: insulated fibres connecting all regions.
white_matter.overview: White matter is made of nerve fibres coated in myelin, a fatty insulation that speeds up signals. It connects areas within each hemisphere, links the two hemispheres through the corpus callosum, and carries signals to and from the brainstem and spinal cord.
functions: Carrying signals to and from the body
clinical: Multiple sclerosis damages myelin in white matter.
Small-vessel disease, more common with age and high blood pressure, can affect white matter.
white_matter.fact: Myelin continues to be added to white matter through childhood and adolescence.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.tagline: The 'little brain' that coordinates movement and balance.
cerebellum.overview: The cerebellum sits at the back of the head below the cerebrum and behind the brainstem. It compares intended movements with what actually happens and fine-tunes them. It has two hemispheres joined by the midline vermis, and also contributes to timing, learning and some thinking skills.
functions: Contributing to some thinking and language
clinical: Damage causes clumsiness, unsteady walking and slurred speech.
Swelling or bleeding here can press on the brainstem and fourth ventricle.
sources: Kandel et al., Principles of Neural Science 6e (2021)

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.tagline: The stalk that links brain and spinal cord and runs vital functions.
brainstem.overview: The brainstem is made of the midbrain, pons and medulla. It carries all signals between the brain and body, contains most cranial nerve nuclei, and houses centres that control breathing, heart rate and wakefulness.
functions: Carrying signals between brain and body
clinical: Brainstem strokes can cause dizziness, double vision and weakness.
Pressure on the brainstem is a medical emergency.
brainstem.fact: Ten of the twelve pairs of cranial nerves attach to the brainstem.

arteries.name: Arteries
arteries.tagline: The vessels that carry oxygen-rich blood to the brain.
arteries.overview: Four arteries carry blood up the neck to the brain: two internal carotid and two vertebral arteries. They join at the base of the brain in the circle of Willis, which gives rise to the anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries.
functions: Providing back-up routes for blood flow
Supplying each brain region through its own branches
clinical: Blocked arteries cause ischaemic stroke.
Aneurysms can form at branch points and may bleed.
arteries.fact: The brain cannot store much energy, so it depends on a constant blood supply.

arteries.overview: The brain receives blood from two internal carotid arteries at the front and two vertebral arteries at the back, which join to form the basilar artery. At the base of the brain, communicating arteries link these into a ring called the circle of Willis. Its shape varies between people, and incomplete circles are common normal variants.

ica.name: Internal carotid artery
ica.supplies: Most of the front and middle of each hemisphere (through the anterior and middle cerebral arteries) and the eye.
ica.note: Arises from the common carotid artery in the neck and enters the skull without branching in the neck.

mca.name: Middle cerebral artery
mca.supplies: The outer surface of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes, the insula and, through small perforating branches, the basal ganglia.
mca.note: The largest branch of the internal carotid artery and the artery most often involved in stroke.

aca.name: Anterior cerebral artery
aca.supplies: The inner surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the leg areas of the motor and touch strips, and most of the corpus callosum.
aca.note: The two anterior cerebral arteries are joined by the anterior communicating artery.

pca.name: Posterior cerebral artery
pca.supplies: The occipital lobe, the underside of the temporal lobe, the thalamus and the midbrain.
pca.note: Usually arises from the top of the basilar artery; in some people it is fed mainly by the internal carotid artery (a 'fetal' pattern), which is a normal variant.

basilar.name: Basilar artery
basilar.supplies: The pons and parts of the cerebellum, then divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries.
basilar.note: Formed where the two vertebral arteries join at the front of the brainstem.

vertebral.name: Vertebral artery
vertebral.supplies: The medulla and lower cerebellum (including via the posterior inferior cerebellar artery), then joins its partner to form the basilar artery.
vertebral.note: Runs up through openings in the neck vertebrae; the two sides are often unequal in size, which is usually normal.

acom.name: Anterior communicating artery
acom.supplies: Small branches to nearby deep structures; mainly connects the two anterior cerebral arteries.
acom.note: A common site of brain aneurysms.

pcom.name: Posterior communicating artery
pcom.supplies: Small branches to the thalamus and hypothalamus; mainly connects the internal carotid to the posterior cerebral artery.
pcom.note: Its size varies widely; an aneurysm here can press on the nerve that moves the eye and lifts the eyelid.

common_carotid.name: Common carotid artery
common_carotid.supplies: Divides in the neck into the internal carotid (brain and eye) and external carotid (face and scalp) arteries.
common_carotid.note: The left usually arises directly from the aortic arch and the right from the brachiocephalic trunk.

eca.name: External carotid artery
eca.supplies: The face, scalp, jaw, throat and the coverings of the brain (via the middle meningeal artery).
eca.note: Its branches can form connections with the internal carotid system.

T1.name: T1-weighted MRI
T1.what: An MRI image in which fat appears bright and fluid appears dark, giving a clear picture of anatomy.
T1.why: Shows the shape of brain structures well; often repeated after a contrast injection to look for areas that light up.

T2.name: T2-weighted MRI
T2.what: An MRI image in which fluid appears bright.
T2.why: Good at showing fluid, swelling and many kinds of tissue change.

FLAIR.name: FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery)
FLAIR.what: A T2-type MRI image in which the normal fluid around and inside the brain is made dark.
FLAIR.why: Makes changes near the ventricles and brain surface easier to see, because the bright fluid no longer hides them.

DWI.name: Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)
DWI.what: An MRI image that measures how freely water molecules move in tissue.
DWI.why: Very sensitive to early stroke and some other conditions in which water movement is restricted.

ADC.name: Apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map
ADC.what: A map calculated from diffusion images that shows water movement as a number for each point.
ADC.why: Read together with DWI to confirm whether water movement is truly restricted.

T2STAR.name: T2* gradient echo (GRE)
T2STAR.what: An MRI image that is sensitive to small disturbances in the magnetic field.
T2STAR.why: Shows blood products, calcium and iron as dark spots.

SWI.name: Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI)
SWI.what: A refined version of T2* imaging that is even more sensitive to magnetic disturbances.
SWI.why: Detects very small amounts of blood, iron or calcium and shows veins clearly.

TOF.name: Time-of-flight MR angiography (TOF MRA)
TOF.what: An MRI technique in which flowing blood appears bright, without needing a contrast injection.
TOF.why: Shows the arteries of the brain and neck, including the circle of Willis.

STIR.name: STIR (short tau inversion recovery)
STIR.what: An MRI image in which fat is made dark and fluid stays bright.
STIR.why: Useful for showing swelling in bones, the spine and soft tissues.

PD.name: Proton density (PD) MRI
PD.what: An MRI image whose brightness mainly reflects how much water (hydrogen) a tissue contains.
PD.why: Often used for joints, such as the knee, to show cartilage and ligaments.

CT.name: Computed tomography (CT)
CT.what: Cross-sectional X-ray images in which each point's brightness reflects tissue density, measured in Hounsfield units.
CT.why: Fast and widely available; good at showing bone and fresh bleeding.

CTA.name: CT angiography (CTA)
CTA.what: A CT scan timed with an iodine contrast injection so the arteries appear bright.
CTA.why: Shows the arteries in detail, including narrowing or bulges.

CR.name: Computed radiography (CR)
CR.what: A digital X-ray taken with a reusable imaging plate that is read by a scanner.
CR.why: A flat (2D) X-ray picture, for example of the chest or bones.

DX.name: Digital radiography (DX)
DX.what: A digital X-ray taken with a detector that produces the image directly.
DX.why: A flat (2D) X-ray picture, for example of the chest or bones.

MIP.name: Maximum intensity projection (MIP)
MIP.what: A view made by a computer from a stack of images, keeping the brightest point along each line of sight.
MIP.why: Shows bright structures such as vessels in angiography as one picture; it is a processed view, not a separate scan.

PHOTO.name: Photo or scanned document
PHOTO.what: A photograph, scanned film or document page imported as an image.
PHOTO.why: Can be viewed, but it has no real-world scale, so no measurements are possible.
